title: IES Recommendations & Conducting a Light-Level Survey

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Classroom at night, shades closed; senior tech unpacks a meter, small stand, tape measure, painter's tape and tablet. Matthew voice-over.
scenes.says: Job Mindset for a light-level survey. Hazards are forklift and vehicle traffic in warehouses and lots, and the urge to climb racking for a vertical reading. Controls: coordinate with the facility, cone off areas, wear hi-vis, and use a proper ladder or MEWP. Plan before you leave: a calibrated meter, stand, tape, grid sheet, and a night visit so daylight doesn't spoil the data.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew in the classroom, medium shot; on-screen typical ranges.
scenes.on_screen:
Targets: IES Recommended Practices; the project specification governs
Open office ~20-40 fc • Classrooms ~30-50 fc • Corridors ~5-10 fc
scenes.says: Targets come from the Illuminating Engineering Society's Recommended Practices, based on the visual task, occupants' age and how important the task is. They're maintained averages on a specified plane, often with uniformity criteria. Typical ranges: open office around 20 to 40 footcandles, classrooms 30 to 50, corridors 5 to 10. Always use the project spec or current IES document for the actual target.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close on meter calibration sticker; cheap meter and phone app set aside.
scenes.on_screen:
Cosine- and color-corrected meter, current calibration
Phone apps can be badly wrong under LED
scenes.says: Use an illuminance meter that's cosine-corrected and color-corrected, with a current calibration, commonly annual. Inexpensive meters and phone apps can be badly wrong under LED spectra. You'll do surveys after retrofits to verify the target, during audits, for 'it's too dark' complaints, and to set high-end trim during commissioning.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech checks the wallstation, overrides dimming to full; clock on wall shows time passing. Matthew voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: 1. Prepare: exclude or subtract daylight • stabilize (LED often 15-30+ min) • controls at full output
scenes.says: Step one: prepare. Survey at night or with shades closed. If you can't exclude daylight, take readings lights-on and lights-off and subtract. Let LED systems run often 15 to 30 minutes or more before reading. Set controls to full output, or state that you measured the as-controlled condition. Note outages, dirty lenses and anything blocking light.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech lays out the grid with tape measure and painter's tape marks on the floor.
scenes.on_screen:
2. Grid: under, between, near walls • ~2 ft from walls • mark it on the plan
3. Plane: work plane 30 in • floor • vertical
scenes.says: Step two: lay out a grid that captures variation: points under fixtures, between them and near walls. Keep points about 2 feet from walls unless wall areas are part of the task, and mark the grid on the plan so it can be repeated. Step three: set the plane. Desks are typically 30 inches. Corridors, warehouses and parking use the floor. Rack faces need vertical readings.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech sets the sensor on a small stand at desk height, steps aside, enters readings into a tablet.
scenes.on_screen: 4. Sensor level • stay out of the light path • dark clothing
scenes.says: Step four: take readings. Hold the sensor level, or use the stand. Stand to the side and keep your body and shadow out of the light path. Dark clothing helps, because light-colored clothing reflects light onto the sensor. Let the reading settle, then record it against the grid point right away.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech holds the sensor 2-4 in from the wall, then turns it around. Graphic: 14 ÷ 30 ≈ 47%.
scenes.says: Step five: estimate reflectances of matte surfaces. Hold the sensor facing the wall 2 to 4 inches away and record. Turn it around at the same spot and record again. Reflected divided by arriving: 14 over 30 is about 47 percent. Take two or three spots per surface, avoid glossy ones, and record ceiling, wall and floor.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tablet screen showing the 12-point data table and results.
scenes.on_screen:
6. Sum 447 ÷ 12 points = 37.3 fc average
Max 47 • Min 29
scenes.says: Step six: calculate and compare. In the sample data, twelve readings sum to 447, so the average is 37.3 footcandles, with a maximum of 47 and a minimum of 29. Compare to the target and note areas above or below. Uniformity comes in the next lesson.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew holding a printed survey report.
scenes.on_screen: Report so someone else can REPEAT the survey
scenes.says: The common mistake is a report nobody can repeat. Include the space, date and time, surveyor, meter model, serial and calibration date, daylight condition, control state, lamp condition, reflectances, grid layout, data, calculations, comparison to target, photos and recommendations. And never stand on equipment or racking to reach a measurement point.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.on_screen: Now read the lesson, take the quiz, then show your evaluator
scenes.says: Calibrated meter, controlled conditions, repeatable grid, honest report. Now read the lesson and take the quiz, then show your evaluator a complete survey.

production_notes: Hands-on demo: senior technician performs the survey at night in a generic classroom or office; presenter voice-over. Props: calibrated illuminance meter with visible calibration sticker, small sensor stand, tape measure, painter's tape, tablet with spreadsheet, report template. On-screen numbers from the lesson's sample data. Closing references hands-on skill LT4-S02 (light-level survey and report).
